items.title: Burrill Crohn interviewed by Monk Rowe, Woodstock, New York, January 3, 2012
items.q: I did a film in 1981, it had nothing to do with jazz, it was called Anne Frank and Maine.

ctx.x: At what point did you start going to live things and looking at them as a cameraman, or as a future documentary filmmaker.

Not until I started doing it I don’t think. I mean I really didn’t think that way until I suddenly got the urge. I did a film in 1981, it had nothing to do with jazz, it was called Anne Frank and Maine. A friend of mine was teaching the Holocaust at a little school with Gentile children in Maine, and he brought in the Holocaust as curriculum. And I thought that was just brilliant. And so I pitched the Anti-Defamation League and I got some money to go up there and make a film. And I didn’t shoot or anything at…

three chip cameras, we shot on one inch tape back then. But I just had a vision of myself having one of these and walking around the street. And one thing led to another and eventually — it was not that one but something like that. But it wasn’t until I started shooting on the portapak that I got a taste of doing that. But it wasn’t for a while until, actually the budgets changed and I had to learn how to do this myself.
